name: Indus Valley Civilisation
title: The story of the Indus Valley Civilisation

text: More than 4,500 years ago, people built great cities beside the Indus river, in today’s Pakistan and north-western India.
Their lands covered more ground than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia put together.
src: c. 2600 BCE: The mature phase begins: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and other cities are laid out with grid streets and drains / in most of present-day Pakistan and north-western India
it covered more ground than Egypt and Mesopotamia together

text: Their streets ran in straight lines, and many brick houses had a place to wash and a toilet.
Covered drains carried the waste away, and the city of Mohenjo-daro had more than 700 wells.
src: Its builders laid out streets on a grid / Houses of baked or mud brick / Many had a bathing platform and a latrine
whose waste ran into covered brick drains along the streets, and Mohenjo-daro had more than 700 wells

text: Traders sailed by sea to Mesopotamia, where people called the Indus land Meluhha.
Mesopotamians even needed translators, people who change words from one language into another, to deal with them.
src: trade by sea with Mesopotamia / Mesopotamian texts that call it Meluhha
Mesopotamians needed translators to deal with traders from the Indus

text: Carvers made small stone seals showing an animal and a line of signs.
Nobody can read their writing yet, so we still do not know what language they spoke.
src: The seals are masterpieces of miniature carving: squares of steatite a few centimetres across, cut in reverse with an animal and a line of signs
No text has been read / the language they record is unknown

text: A small stone statue of a bearded man, nicknamed the Priest-King, is one of their few stone sculptures.
No palaces or royal tombs have been found, so who ruled the cities is still a puzzle.
src: Stone sculpture is rare; the best known is the steatite bust nicknamed the “Priest-King”, 17.5 centimetres high, showing a bearded man
No palaces, royal tombs or monuments celebrating conquest have been found / Who governed these cities is unknown

text: About 3,900 years ago the cities began to empty, but the people lived on in smaller villages.
Today the ruins of Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira are World Heritage Sites.
src: From about 1900 BCE the cities declined / The people did not disappear / lived on in smaller villages until about 1300 BCE
Mohenjo-daro became a World Heritage Site in 1980 and Dholavira in 2021
